pages.text:
PRINCIPLES OF PATHOLOGIC REVIEW

Pathologic Evaluation
• Mesothelioma originates from the cells in the serosal lining that surrounds the body cavities. Of all mesotheliomas, ~85% arise from the 
pleura, ~15% arise from the peritoneum, and the remainder (<1%) originate from the pericardium or the tunica vaginalis.1 
• In the United States, diffuse pleural mesothelioma affects ~3,000 patients each year, with an annual incidence of ~1 in 100,000.2,3
• The purpose of the pathologic evaluation of mesothelioma is based on the pathologic assessment of tumor tissue, which can be obtained 
from core biopsy sampling, pleurectomy, or other more extensive resections such as extrapleural pneumonectomy (EPP). Given its rarity 
and overlapping microscopic features with other conditions, the histologic diagnosis of diffuse mesothelioma can be challenging. 
• To establish a pathologic diagnosis of mesothelioma, diagnostic tools that are used clinically include histologic assessment, 
immunohistochemistry (IHC), cytogenetics, and molecular techniques (eg, targeted next-generation sequencing [NGS], fluorescence in 
situ hybridization [FISH], single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays). Despite the multiple diagnostic toolkits, the diagnosis relies primarily on 
proper histologic assessment and IHC.
• The new edition of the World Health Organization (WHO) Classification of Thoracic Tumors by the International Agency for Research on 
Cancer (IARC) introduced the following changes for 2021 from the previous 2015 edition1,4:
New entity: mesothelioma in situ
New terminology: diffuse pleural mesothelioma (instead of diffuse malignant pleural mesothelioma)
New terminology: localized pleural mesothelioma (instead of localized malignant pleural mesothelioma)
New terminology: well-differentiated papillary mesothelial tumor (WDPMT, instead of well-differentiated papillary mesothelioma)
Genetic tumor syndromes involving the thorax: BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome is a hereditary cancer syndrome caused by 

heterozygous germline pathogenic variants in the BAP1 gene.
• The descriptions below refer to diffuse mesothelioma, which will be named mesothelioma for the purpose of simplicity.

Mesothelioma Classification
• Mesothelioma is classified into three histologic types: epithelioid, biphasic (mixed), and sarcomatoid, which have significant prognostic 
value.1
• The determination of histologic types is based on the cytologic features of the tumor:
Epithelioid mesothelioma is characterized by epithelioid-to-round cells.
Sarcomatoid mesothelioma is characterized by spindled cells with tapered nuclei.
Biphasic mesothelioma contains both epithelioid and sarcomatoid components in various proportions, with each comprising at least 10% 

of the tumor. 

References

PRINCIPLES OF PATHOLOGIC REVIEW

Mesothelioma Classification (continued)
• Within each histologic type, mesothelioma can be divided into several subtypes and patterns based on its cytologic, architectural, and 
background stromal features.5 
Other rare variants of epithelioid mesothelioma include clear cell, signet ring cell, rhabdoid, deciduoid, and small cell.6-8 Tumor cells are 

arranged in diverse architectural patterns that include tubulopapillary, trabecular, solid, acinar, micropapillary, or adenomatoid.
In sarcomatoid mesothelioma, subtypes described include conventional/spindle cell, desmoplastic,9,10 and lymphohistiocytoid.11-13 

A subset of sarcomatoid mesothelioma exhibits heterologous differentiation with osteosarcomatous, chondrosarcomatous, and/or 
rhabdomyosarcomatous elements.10
The assignment of histologic type can be challenging, given the intertumoral and intratumoral morphologic heterogeneity. Appropriate type 

classification of mesothelioma is nonetheless important, given the prognostic significance of different histologic types.
Studies comparing the concordance between histologic type in initial biopsies with subsequent resections have shown that the accuracy 

of typing increases with a higher number of biopsies.14 While sarcomatoid histology in biopsies is highly predictive of sarcomatoid 
histology in resections, epithelioid histology in biopsies is not entirely specific and is changed to biphasic or sarcomatoid types in 
resections in up to 20% of patients.14
Histologic Criteria for Mesothelioma
• In mesothelioma, the goals of histologic assessment are to confirm the pathologic diagnosis and to determine the histologic type, which 
allows for prognostication and treatment planning. For the diagnosis of mesothelioma, one needs to establish each of the three conditions 
below:
The lesion is diffuse and not solitary. Correlation with clinical and radiologic findings is needed to confirm that the distribution of the tumor 

is diffuse rather than solitary. While almost all (>99%) mesotheliomas are diffuse, rare cases of localized pleural mesothelioma have been 
described, which are solitary, have a different pathogenesis, and harbor a relatively less aggressive clinical course.15-18
The lesional cells are mesothelial. Given the morphologic overlap between mesothelioma and diverse mimics such as carcinomas, IHC can 

be used to confirm the presence of mesothelial differentiation in the tumor cells. Other tools such as cytogenetics and molecular analysis 
may also be helpful in some instances (see next page).
The lesional cells are malignant. Histologic assessment is integral to establish that the mesothelial cells are malignant. Morphologic 

features that distinguish mesothelioma from reactive conditions include: 1) invasion into adjacent tissue, such as adipose or fibrous 
tissue, and skeletal muscle; 2) full-thickness serosal involvement; and 3) formation of expansile nodules (considered as a type of fibrous 
tissue invasion). The presence of tissue invasion is considered to be the most reliable criterion in distinguishing mesothelioma from 
reactive mesothelial proliferations.19,20 On the other hand, “worrisome” features such as necrosis, cytologic atypia, and mitoses should be 
interpreted with caution, since each can be present in reactive pleuritis and do not necessarily indicate malignancy.
• Interpretation can be difficult when there is limited diagnostic tissue, tangential sectioning, artifacts from histologic processing, and/
or entrapment of adjacent structures mimicking invasion.19,21 For a mesothelial proliferation that is suspicious for, but not definitive for 
malignancy, one may report the findings as “atypical mesothelial proliferation” and recommend rebiopsy and/or close follow-up.
• In the distinction between mesothelioma and benign, reactive mesothelial proliferations, the role of ancillary studies has been limited until 
recently, where BAP1 or MTAP IHC and CDKN2A copy number assessment by FISH may aid in the distinction in some instances (see next 
page).22 

References

pages.text:
PRINCIPLES OF PATHOLOGIC REVIEW

Immunohistochemistry
Markers to Confirm Mesothelial Differentiation
• IHC is integral to the pathologic diagnosis of mesothelioma in clinical practice.
• Useful IHC markers include: 1) positive markers to confirm mesothelial differentiation, such as WT1, calretinin, and D2-40; and 2) negative 
markers to exclude mimics, such as polyclonal carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), and claudin-4.23-25 
One of the caveats is that no individual IHC marker is entirely sensitive and specific. Therefore, it is recommended that a panel including at 
least two mesothelial markers (eg, calretinin, WT1, D2-40) and two carcinoma markers (eg, claudin-4, TTF-1, polyclonal CEA) should be used 
to establish the diagnosis.26
• Broad-spectrum keratins (eg, AE1/AE3, pancytokeratin, MNF116) are not specific and are expressed in both mesothelioma and carcinomas. 
• Sarcomatoid mesothelioma often shows focal to absent expression for most mesothelial markers, with the most sensitive marker being 
D2-40/podoplanin.27 
• Recently, GATA3 has been explored as a potential diagnostic marker for sarcomatoid mesotheliomas since GATA3 is expressed in only ~10% to 
20% of sarcomatoid carcinoma28 and strongly expressed in all sarcomatoid/desmoplastic mesotheliomas.29

Markers to Confirm a Mesothelial Malignant Proliferation
• Although the distinction between diffuse or localized mesothelioma and reactive mesothelial proliferations primarily relies on histologic 
assessment, this can be challenging in some cases. 
• BAP1, MTAP IHC, and CDKN2A (p16) FISH are established markers for diagnosing mesothelioma.22 
BAP1 IHC is a specific (though not sensitive) marker to distinguish mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations. 
BAP1 is a tumor suppressor implicated in the pathogenesis of mesothelioma, uveal melanoma, cholangiocarcinoma, and clear cell renal 

cell carcinoma.30 Recurrent somatic and/or germline mutations in BAP1 are present in mesothelioma. As a surrogate for BAP1 genomic 
status, BAP1 IHC is used as a diagnostic marker for mesothelioma, whereas reactive proliferations have intact BAP1 nuclear staining. 
Complete absence of expression or cytoplasmic staining is considered a loss of BAP1 expression. Aberrant BAP1 protein expression, 
defined as absence of nuclear BAP1 staining, is present in ~50% to 70% of mesothelioma epithelioid type31-37 but in <20% of sarcomatoid 
type.38
MTAP IHC has been used as a diagnostic marker for mesothelioma.39 MTAP is located near CDKN2A on the chromosomal region 9p21. 

Loss of cytoplasmic MTAP staining is considered a surrogate for chromosomal 9p loss as determined by concurrent CDKN2A FISH 
testing39 and has been reported in ~40% to 60% of mesothelioma but rarely in reactive proliferations.35-37 
Although MTAP alone is not sensitive, combined use of BAP1 and MTAP IHC may improve sensitivity and specificity.35-37 Since ~10% to 

20% of lung adenocarcinomas have MTAP loss,36 MTAP IHC is not useful for distinction between mesothelioma and lung carcinoma.
• Additional IHC markers such as 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC), enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), cyclin D1, and programmed death 
ligand 1 (PD-L1), and NF2 by FISH are all potentially useful to distinguish mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations, but need 
further study since their utility in clinical practice remains unclear.22 

References

pages.text:
PRINCIPLES OF PATHOLOGIC REVIEW

Immunohistochemistry (continued)
Markers as Potential Prognostic and Predictive Markers
• Recent studies explored IHC targets as potential prognostic and predictive markers.
Patients with pleural mesothelioma, epithelioid type, with loss of BAP1 by IHC and retained p16 expression by IHC have prolonged survival 

in both univariate and multivariate analyses.40 
Patients with mesothelioma with germline BAP1 mutations have a prolonged survival.41,42
ALK rearrangements by IHC found in rare patients with peritoneal mesothelioma43-46 have shown dramatic response with ALK inhibitor 

therapies.47,48 
• PD-L1 (CD274), a negative regulator of immune checkpoint, represents a target in immunotherapy, with PD-L1 IHC evaluated as a predictive 
biomarker in diverse tumor types.49
• The utility of PD-L1 IHC as a predictive marker for immune checkpoint inhibitors and the optimal assessment criteria in mesothelioma remain 
unclear.

Cytogenetic Features
• Most mesotheliomas are characterized by complex numerical and structural karyotypic alterations.50 
• Although no specific chromosomal abnormalities are pathognomonic for mesothelioma, loss of chromosomal region 9p including CDKN2A 
or 22q including NF2 is noted in a subset of tumors. 
Homozygous loss of CDKN2A by FISH testing is present in ~60% of mesotheliomas.51-53 
While detection of CDKN2A loss can aid in the distinction of mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations, CDKN2A loss alone is 

not useful in separating mesothelioma from other tumor types, since CDKN2A loss can be found in a substantial fraction of sarcomatoid 
mesotheliomas, sarcomatoid carcinomas, and sarcomas.54 
Hemizygous loss of NF2 by FISH is present in ~50% of pleural mesotheliomas.55 
• A rare subset of pleural mesothelioma harbors a peculiar near-haploid karyotype, with extensive loss of heterozygosity involving nearly all 
chromosomes except chromosomes 5 and 7.56 

Molecular Features
• Most mesotheliomas are characterized by recurrent mutations in tumor suppressors and epigenetic regulators, including BAP1, NF2, TP53, 
SETD2, and other genes.56-60 Consistent with its histomorphologic heterogeneity, mesothelioma shows an impressive molecular diversity.
• Alterations are identified in multiple pathways in the regulation of cell cycle, RNA processing, histone regulation, and cell growth.58 BAP1 
is one of the most frequently altered genes; mechanisms of BAP1 inactivation include point mutations, copy number loss, inactivating 
structural rearrangements, and minute chromosomal deletions.56-58,61-63
• Furthermore, a small subset of pleural mesothelioma harbors unusual genetic alterations: Genomic near-haploidization was described in 
rare pleural mesotheliomas that harbor mutations in TP53 and/or SETDB1.56 
• Peritoneal mesothelioma has distinct molecular features compared to pleural mesothelioma.64

References

pages.title: Mesothelioma: Pleural
pages.text:
PRINCIPLES OF PATHOLOGIC REVIEW

Molecular Features (continued)
• Oncogenic EWSR1::ATF1 fusion has been described in pleural and peritoneal mesotheliomas in young adults.64,65 
ALK rearrangements have been identified in rare patients with peritoneal mesothelioma.43-45,48
• Germline mutations are overall present in 12%–16% of patients with pleural and peritoneal mesotheliomas and primarily involve genes 
in the DNA repair and cell cycle regulation, such as BAP1, BRCA2, CDKN2A, TMEM127, VHL, WT1, MRE11A, and MSH6.42,66,67 Germline 
mutations appear to be more common in patients who are young, have a family history of mesothelioma, or have a clinical history of other 
synchronous malignancies.42,66,68

Differential Diagnosis
• The differential diagnosis of mesothelioma depends on the histologic type (epithelioid, biphasic, or sarcomatoid) under consideration. 
Mesothelioma can resemble reactive pleuritis or diverse tumor types, including carcinomas, melanomas, and sarcomas. 
• In addition to diffuse mesothelioma, WHO recognizes additional types of mesothelial lesions: 1) localized mesothelioma, 2) WDPMT, and 3) 
adenomatoid tumor.1
Localized pleural mesothelioma is microscopically identical to mesothelioma, although it is radiographically and grossly solitary and 

circumscribed.15-17 Genetically, localized pleural mesothelioma includes three groups (BAP1-mutant, TRAF7-mutant, and near-haploid), 
with similarities but also differences from pleural mesothelioma.18 
WDPMT, often an incidental finding in the peritoneum of those assigned female at birth, can occur in the pleura,69 and is genetically 

characterized by recurrent mutations in TRAF7 or CDC42.70 Infrequently, WDPMT shows back-to-back papillae with foci of invasion,71 
morphologically mimicking mesothelioma. Furthermore, distinction between a mesothelioma with prominent papillary surface projections 
and WDPMT can be challenging, particularly in small superficial biopsies. 
Adenomatoid tumor primarily affects the genital tracts but rarely can involve the pleura; recurrent mutations in TRAF7 have been described 

in adenomatoid tumors of genital type.72
Peritoneal inclusion cyst is a benign, rare tumor that displays multiple mesothelial-lined cysts that may be distinguished from mesothelial 

neoplasia. This lesion is almost always located in the peritoneum, although uncommon cases have been described in the pleura. These 
cystic proliferations are lined by bland mesothelial cells and lack significant stratification, papillary structures, or atypia.
Mesothelioma in situ is a preinvasive, single-layer surface proliferation of neoplastic mesothelial cells. Since the diagnosis of 

mesothelioma in situ cannot be simply made on conventional hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stains, the diagnosis requires either 1) loss of 
BAP1 nuclear expression by IHC; and/or 2) CDKN2A homozygous deletion identified either by FISH or by MTAP IHC (cytoplasmic staining). 
Furthermore, no mass lesions should be identified on imaging or thoracoscopy.

PRINCIPLES OF SUPPORTIVE CARE AND SURVIVORSHIP

• Pleural effusions: Talc pleurodesis or pleural catheter, if required for management of pleural effusion.a Drainage is preferred for candidates 
with potentially operable disease; drainage or pleurodesis are both options for patients with inoperable disease.

• Radiotherapy and image-guided thermal ablation1 are palliative options for symptomatic pleural disease. 

• Pain management: NCCN Guidelines for Adult Cancer Pain 

• Nausea/vomiting: NCCN Guidelines for Antiemesis

• Psychosocial distress: NCCN Guidelines for Distress Management 

• Fatigue: NCCN Guidelines for Cancer-Related Fatigue 

• Immunotherapy-related toxicities: NCCN Guidelines for the Management of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Related Toxicities 

• Venous thromboembolic disease: NCCN Guidelines for Cancer-Associated Venous Thromboembolic Disease

• NCCN Guidelines for Palliative Care as indicated 

• Smoking cessation counseling and intervention: NCCN Guidelines for Smoking Cessation; NCCN Guidelines for Lung Cancer Screening 

• Survivorship: NCCN Guidelines for Survivorship

a If FDG-PET/CT is to be done, recommend obtaining FDG-PET/CT before pleurodesis. Confirm diagnosis of pleural mesothelioma prior to pleurodesis. If pleural 

mesothelioma is suspected, consider evaluation by a multidisciplinary team with expertise in pleural mesothelioma.

PRINCIPLES OF RADIATION THERAPY

General Principles
• Recommendations regarding RT should be made by radiation oncologists with experience in managing pleural mesothelioma. 
• The best timing for delivering RT after surgical intervention and/or in conjunction with chemotherapy should be discussed by a 
multidisciplinary team including radiation oncologists, surgeons, medical oncologists, diagnostic imaging specialists, and pulmonologists. 
• PET scanning for treatment planning can be used as indicated.
• Prophylactic RT is not routinely recommended to prevent instrument-tract recurrence after pleural intervention.1
• RT is an effective palliative treatment for relief of chest pain, bronchial or esophageal obstruction, or other symptomatic sites associated 
with mesothelioma. 
• A randomized phase III trial in patients with non-metastatic pleural mesothelioma who underwent non-radical lung-sparing surgery found 
substantially greater overall survival with sequential pleural intensity-modulated RT (IMRT) compared to palliative RT.2 Sequential pleural 
IMRT after P/D in the presence of an intact lung may be considered in centers with experience and expertise in these methods, given the 
technical difficulty of this treatment.3-5 
• Advanced technologies may be used, such as image-guided RT (IGRT) for treatment involving IMRT/stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS)/
stereotactic body RT (SBRT), and intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT).6 
Radiation Dose and Volume 
• The dose of radiation should be based on the purpose of the treatment. See Recommended Doses for Radiation Therapy (PM-D 2 of 3).
• A dose ≥60 Gy should be delivered to macroscopic residual tumors if the doses to adjacent normal structures are limited to their tolerances. 
In addition to covering the surgical bed within the thorax, the volume of postoperative radiation should also include the surgical scars and 
biopsy tracks in the chest wall.7-9
• Daily doses of 4 Gy appear to be more efficacious than fractions of <4 Gy in providing relief from chest pain associated with 
mesothelioma,8,10 although the optimal daily and total dose of RT for palliative purposes remains unclear. 
• For patients with residual tumors, some experienced investigators have used brachytherapy or intraoperative external beam RT (EBRT) in 
combination with surgery.

• Use of highly conformal radiation technology (IMRT) is the preferred choice based on comprehensive consideration of target coverage and 
clinically relevant normal tissue tolerance.4,11 Advanced technologies are appropriate when needed to deliver curative RT safely. These 
technologies include (but are not limited to) 4D-CT and/or PET/CT simulation, IMRT/volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), IGRT, motion 
management, and proton therapy.
• Special attention should be paid to minimize radiation to the contralateral lung,12 as the risk of fatal pneumonitis with IMRT is excessively 
high when strict limits are not applied.13 The contralateral uninvolved mean lung dose (MLD) should be kept as low as possible, preferably 
<8.5 Gy. The low-dose volume should be minimized.14 For postoperative RT for patients who have P/D, other recommended specific lung-
preserving techniques are advised. Limit the ipsilateral lung dose to decrease risk of pneumonitis and keep total MLD <21 Gy and V20 <40% 
and contralateral lung V20 <7% and MLD <8 Gy.15 
• The gross tumor volume (GTV) should include any grossly visible tumor. Surgical clips (indicative of gross residual tumor) should be 
included for postoperative adjuvant RT.
• The clinical target volume (CTV) for adjuvant RT after P/D should encompass the entire pleural surface (for partial resection cases), surgical 
clips, and any potential sites with residual disease. 
• Extensive elective nodal irradiation (ENI) (entire mediastinum and bilateral supraclavicular nodal regions) is not recommended.
• The planning target volume (PTV) should consider the target motion and daily setup errors. The PTV margin should be based on the 
individual patient's motion, simulation techniques used (with and without inclusion motion), and reproducibility of each clinic’s daily setup.

PRINCIPLES OF SURGERY1

• Surgical resection should be performed on carefully evaluated patients by thoracic surgeons with experience in managing pleural 
mesothelioma.
• Decisions regarding surgical options for treatment are highly dependent on accurate histology. Pleural biopsy for diagnosis should provide 
enough tissue for differentiation of epithelioid, sarcomatoid, or mixed histology and clearly exclude metastatic pleural involvement of 
another primary. Cytology is generally not considered adequate for important histologic differentiation required for treatment decisions.
• For patients being considered for surgery, a single-port thoracoscopy on the line of the potential incision is recommended.
• The goal of surgery is complete gross cytoreduction of the tumor. The goal of cytoreductive surgery is “macroscopic complete resection”—in 
other words, removal of ALL visible or palpable tumors. In cases where this is not possible, such as in multiple sites of chest wall invasion, 
surgery should be aborted. If it is possible to remove most of the gross disease to help with postoperative management, with a minimal 
impact on morbidity, then surgery should be continued. 
• The surgical choices are: 1) P/D with mediastinal lymph node sampling, which is defined as complete removal of the pleura and all gross tumor 
± en-bloc resection of pericardium and/or diaphragm with reconstruction; and 2) EPP, which is defined as en-bloc resection of the pleura, lung, 
ipsilateral diaphragm, and often pericardium. Mediastinal node sampling should be performed with a goal to obtain at least 3 nodal stations.
• For early-stage disease (confined to the pleural envelope, no clinical evidence for lymph node involvement) with favorable histology 
(epithelioid), P/D may be considered but it is unclear whether there is benefit over systemic therapy alone. There is controversy regarding a 
decision for surgical resection that needs to be weighed, taking into account tumor histology, distribution, the patient's pulmonary reserve, and 
availability of adjuvant and intraoperative strategies. P/D is the preferred surgical treatment option and can be considered in select patients for 
complete gross cytoreduction. EPP may be selected in certain cases that require careful consideration of the total treatment plan that includes 
the patient and multidisciplinary team.2-5
• If N2 disease is identified, prognosis with surgery (and other therapy) is substantially diminished. Surgical resection should only be considered 
in the setting of a clinical trial or at a center with expertise in pleural mesothelioma.
• If technically appropriate for even more advanced disease, lung-sparing operations like P/D reduce the risk for perioperative mortality and 
may be acceptable in terms of achieving complete macroscopic resection. P/D can provide excellent symptomatic control of recurrent pleural 
effusions.
• Intraoperative adjuvant therapy is still under investigation but may be considered as part of a reasonable multidisciplinary approach to this 
locally aggressive disease.
• After recovery from surgery, patients should be referred for adjuvant therapy, which may include chemotherapy and RT depending on whether 
any preoperative therapy was used and on the pathologic analysis of the surgical specimen.

Overview 

Guidelines update, using the search term: pleural mesothelioma. The 
PubMed database was chosen because it remains the most widely used 
resource for medical literature and indexes peer-reviewed biomedical 
literature.17 

The search results were narrowed by selecting studies in humans 
published in English. Results were confined to the following article types: 
Clinical Trial, Phase II; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Clinical Trial, Phase IV; 
Guideline; Practice Guideline; Randomized Controlled Trial; Meta-
Analysis; Systematic Reviews; and Validation Studies. The data from key 
PubMed articles as well as articles from additional sources deemed as 
relevant to these Guidelines as discussed by the Panel during the 
Guidelines update have been included in this version of the Discussion 
section. Recommendations for which high-level evidence is lacking are 
based on the Panel’s review of lower-level evidence and expert opinion. 

Mesothelioma is a rare cancer originating from mesothelial surfaces of the 
pleura and other sites that is estimated to occur in approximately 3000 
people in the United States every year.1,2 Although the incidence has 
stabilized in the United States in recent years, mesothelioma diagnoses 
continue to increase worldwide.3 Pleural mesothelioma (PM), historically 
referred to as malignant pleural mesothelioma, is the most common type 
(approximately 85%); however, mesothelioma can also occur in the lining 
of other sites, such as the peritoneum (approximately 15%), pericardium, 
and tunica vaginalis testis.2,4,5 PM is difficult to treat, as most patients have 
advanced disease at presentation.6,7 Median overall survival (OS) is 
approximately 1 year after diagnosis of PM, and 5-year OS is about 5% to 
10%.7-14 Most patients diagnosed with PM are >60 years of age.6,9 PM 
occurs mainly in males who have been exposed to asbestos, although 
diagnosis may occur decades after exposure.6,7,15,16 For example, it has 
been estimated that the median latent period is >32 years.15 

Sensitive/Inclusive Language Usage 

These NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN 
Guidelines®) provide recommendations for the evaluation and treatment of 
patients diagnosed with PM. The Guidelines were developed and are 
updated by Panel members who also update the NCCN Guidelines for 
Mesothelioma: Peritoneal and the NCCN Guidelines for Non-Small Cell 
Lung Cancer. 

Guidelines Update Methodology 

The complete details of the Development and Update of the NCCN 
Guidelines are available at www.NCCN.org. 

Literature Search Criteria 

NCCN Guidelines strive to use language that advances the goals of 
equity, inclusion, and representation.18 NCCN Guidelines endeavor to use 
language that is person-first; not stigmatizing; anti-racist, anti-classist, anti-
misogynist, anti-ageist, anti-ableist, and anti-weight biased; and inclusive 
of individuals of all sexual orientations and gender identities. NCCN 
Guidelines incorporate non-gendered language, instead focusing on 
organ-specific recommendations. This language is both more accurate 
and more inclusive and can help fully address the needs of individuals of 
all sexual orientations and gender identities. NCCN Guidelines will 
continue to use the terms men, women, female, and male when citing 
statistics, recommendations, or data from organizations or sources that do 
not use inclusive terms. Most studies do not report how sex and gender 
data are collected and use these terms interchangeably or inconsistently. 
If sources do not differentiate gender from sex assigned at birth or organs 
present, the information is presumed to predominantly represent cisgender 

Prior to the annual update of the NCCN Guidelines for Mesothelioma: 
Pleural, an electronic search of the PubMed database was performed to 
obtain key literature in pleural mesothelioma published since the previous

Risk Factors 

Smoking is not considered a risk factor for mesothelioma.53,54 However, 
patients who smoke and have been exposed to asbestos are at increased 
risk for lung cancer.55,56 Patients who smoke should be encouraged to quit 
because it may negatively affect treatment.57 Please refer to the NCCN 
Guidelines for Smoking Cessation, available at www.NCCN.org. 

Exposure to asbestos is the primary risk factor for PM.5,19,20 Most 
mesotheliomas are associated with occupational exposure to asbestos; 
however, individuals with non-occupational exposure also have increased 
risk.21-23 Some patients exposed to asbestos may only have benign pleural 
disease.24,25 

Although screening for mesothelioma has been studied in patients at high 
risk (ie, those with asbestos exposure), the NCCN Guidelines do not 
recommend screening for PM because it has not been shown to decrease 
mortality.55,58-64 Note that the NCCN Guidelines for Lung Cancer Screening 
with low-dose CT do not apply to PM as there are no data to suggest that 
screening with low-dose CT improves survival for patients with PM.55,61,65-68 

Diagnosis 

Presentation and Evaluation 

Other risk factors for PM have been identified. Patients exposed to 
ionizing radiation are thought to be at increased risk of developing 
mesothelioma.20,26-37 One study that evaluated 47,219 patients with 
Hodgkin lymphoma and 252,090 patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma 
from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database 
found that patients treated with radiation therapy (RT) had a higher risk of 
developing mesothelioma as a secondary malignancy than those who 
were not irradiated.26 Another risk factor is erionite, a naturally occurring 
fiber-like mineral that is more potent than asbestos; however, fewer people 
are at risk of developing mesothelioma from erionite as it is only found in 
certain geographic locations and is generally not used for commercial 
applications.38-42 

Patients with suspected PM often have dyspnea and chest wall pain; they 
may also have pleural effusion, fatigue, insomnia, cough, chest wall mass, 
loss of appetite, and weight loss.5,54,69,70 Patients with PM may have a high 
symptom burden when compared with patients who have other types of 
cancer. Most patients present without distant metastases, and central 
nervous system (CNS) metastases are rare.71 

In patients with recurrent pleural effusion and/or pleural thickening, the 
recommended initial evaluation for suspected PM includes: 1) chest CT 
with contrast; 2) thoracentesis for cytologic assessment; and 3) pleural 
biopsy (eg, thoracoscopic biopsy [preferred], CT-guided core biopsy, open 
biopsy) (see PM-1 in the algorithm).69,72-79 However, cytologic samples are 
often negative even when patients have PM.80,81 Soluble 

Genetic factors may also play a role in PM.38,43-52 For example, a high 
incidence of PM has been reported in a small number of families in the 
absence of exposure to occupational asbestos or erionite; germline 
mutations in the BAP1 gene were identified as a risk factor.52 Interestingly, 
some studies reported that patients with PM and deleterious germline 
BAP1 mutations have prolonged survival compared to those with wild-type 
BAP1.47,50 Genetic counseling and germline testing may be warranted for 
patients with a young age at diagnosis, personal or family history

pages.text:

these levels may correlate with disease status.82-85 

rare cases of localized mesothelioma have been diagnosed, which are 
less aggressive.97-101 Distinguishing malignant disease from benign pleural 
disease (such as reactive pleuritis) and from other types of malignancies, 
such as carcinomas, melanomas, and sarcomas, can also be 
challenging.102-105 

Pleurodesis or pleural catheter may be needed for management of pleural 
effusion (see Principles of Supportive Care and Survivorship in the 
algorithm).86-94 Drainage can be pursued in patients who are awaiting 
systemic therapy, including use of indwelling tunneled pleural catheters.86 
Patients should be assessed for distress. Refer to the NCCN Distress 
Thermometer and Problem List within the NCCN Guidelines for Distress 
Management (DIS-A) at www.NCCN.org. 

Pathology 

The goals of the pathologic evaluation of mesothelioma are to confirm the 
pathologic diagnosis and to determine histology. The diagnostic tools used 
include histologic assessment, immunohistochemistry (IHC), cytogenetics, 
and molecular techniques (eg, targeted next-generation sequencing 
[NGS], fluorescence in situ hybridization [FISH], single-nucleotide 
polymorphism arrays). However, the diagnosis relies primarily on proper 
histologic assessment and IHC. 

IHC can be used to confirm mesothelial differentiation and mesothelial 
malignant proliferation. Cytologic samples of pleural fluid are often 
negative or inconclusive, but diagnosis can sometimes be made using 
cytology.80,81,106,107 IHC markers used to confirm mesothelioma 
differentiation include markers specific for mesothelial differentiation (eg, 
WT1, calretinin, D2-40) and markers that typically are positive in 
carcinoma and negative in mesothelioma (eg, thyroid transcription factor 1 
[TTF-1], polyclonal carcinoembryonic antigen [CEA], claudin-4) (see 
Principles of Pathologic Review in the algorithm).4,108-111 A panel of two 
positive mesothelial markers and two negative carcinoma markers is 
recommended for diagnosis of mesothelioma.4 The presence or absence 
of BAP1 nuclear expression assessed by IHC can also be used in the 
diagnosis of mesothelioma.4,112,113 MTAP IHC and CDKN2A (p16) FISH 
are other established markers that can be used to inform a mesothelioma 
diagnosis.4 Other markers may also be useful in establishing mesothelial 
malignant proliferation, but additional data are needed.114 

There are three histologic subtypes of mesothelioma according to the 
World Health Organization (WHO) histologic classification system based 
on cytologic features: epithelioid, sarcomatoid, and biphasic (mixed with 
both epithelioid and sarcomatoid components, with each comprising ≥10% 
of the tumor).95 Epithelioid histology is the most common type and has a 
more favorable prognosis than biphasic or sarcomatoid histologies.9,96 
Assignment of histologic type can be challenging given the intertumoral 
and intratumoral morphologic heterogeneity; however, it is essential to 
determine the histology for prognostication and treatment planning 
purposes. 

Most mesotheliomas are characterized by complex karyotypic alterations 
as well as by recurrent mutations in tumor suppressors and epigenetic 
regulators. Rare genetic alterations such as EWSR1-ATF1 fusions, TP53, 
NF2, SETDB1, or SETD2 mutations have been found in patients with 
PM.115-120 NTRK and ALK gene fusions have also been identified.121-123 
PMs generally have distinct molecular features compared with peritoneal 
mesotheliomas.124 

It is sometimes difficult to distinguish localized mesothelioma from diffuse 
mesothelioma.97 Almost all mesotheliomas are diffuse (>99%); however, 

See the Principles of Pathologic Review section in the algorithm for 
additional information on pathologic evaluation.

Pretreatment Evaluation 

Overview of Treatment Approaches 

Systemic Therapy 

The current Guidelines recommend systemic therapy as the primary 
treatment modality for most patients with PM, regardless of resectability 
(see PM-2 in the algorithm). For the minority of patients who will receive 
cytoreductive surgery, systemic therapy is recommended as either 
induction or adjuvant therapy. 

Once a PM diagnosis is confirmed, patients should be treated by a 
multidisciplinary team with experience in PM (see PM-1 in the algorithm). 
The multidisciplinary team should include diagnostic imaging specialists, 
pulmonologists, surgeons, medical oncologists, and radiation oncologists. 
A chest and abdominal CT with contrast is recommended as part of the 
pretreatment evaluation for staging and to guide treatment strategy for 
patients (see PM-2 in the algorithm).73,74,79,125 

Patients with a diagnosis of clinical stage I PM with epithelioid histology 
may undergo additional testing (see PM-3 in the algorithm), including 1) 
fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-PET/CT; 2) mediastinoscopy or endobronchial 
ultrasound (EBUS)/endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) fine-needle aspiration 
(FNA) of the mediastinal lymph nodes126,127; and 3) optional chest MRI with 
contrast to evaluate possible chest wall, spinal, diaphragmatic, or vascular 
involvement.73,79 Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or 
laparoscopy can be considered if contralateral or peritoneal disease is 
suspected to rule out transdiaphragmatic extension (eg, extension to the 
peritoneum is indicative of stage IV [unresectable] disease).128 

First-Line Therapy 
Historically, cytotoxic chemotherapy has been the primary type of systemic 
therapy used for the treatment of PM. Pemetrexed in combination with 
cisplatin is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as 
an initial treatment for patients with PM whose disease is unresectable or 
who are otherwise not candidates for curative surgery.132 This approval 
was based on data from a phase 3 randomized trial that assessed 
cisplatin/pemetrexed versus cisplatin alone in 456 patients with PM who 
were not candidates for surgery.133 A longer median survival time was 
observed in the cisplatin/pemetrexed group compared with cisplatin alone 
(12.1 vs. 9.3 months, P = .02). 

FDG-PET/CT scans should be obtained before pleurodesis if practical, 
because talc produces pleural inflammation, which can affect FDG avidity 
(ie, false-positive result),129-131 or after drainage of effusion without 
pleurodesis to better evaluate pleural disease burden. 

Carboplatin/pemetrexed was assessed in three separate phase 2 studies; 
the reported median OS ranged from 12.7 to 14 months.134-136 An 
expanded access trial that evaluated cisplatin/pemetrexed or 
carboplatin/pemetrexed in 1704 chemotherapy-naïve patients with 
medically inoperable PM demonstrated that the two regimens resulted in 
similar 1-year survival rates.137 

Patients with clinical stage I PM with epithelioid histology should be 
evaluated to assess whether they can tolerate surgery using pulmonary 
function tests (PFTs), including diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon 
dioxide (DLCO) and cardiac stress tests. 

A multicenter phase 3 randomized trial (IFCT-GFPC-0701 MAPS) 
evaluated the addition of bevacizumab to cisplatin/pemetrexed (with 
maintenance bevacizumab) versus cisplatin/pemetrexed alone for 448 
patients with unresectable PM and performance status (PS) 0 to 2 who 
were chemotherapy-naive and did not have any substantial cardiovascular

A phase 2 open-label study assessed bevacizumab in combination with 
carboplatin/pemetrexed as a first-line therapy in 76 patients with 
unresectable PM.139 The median OS was 15.3 months. A partial response 
was observed in 34.2% (26/76) of patients, while 57.9% (44/76) had stable

hypertension, risk for bleeding or clotting, and substantial cardiovascular

The trial was not powered to assess superiority within the subgroups; 
however, among 455 patients with epithelioid histology, the median OS 
was 18.2 months in those receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus 
16.7 months in those receiving chemotherapy (HR, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.69 to 
1.03]).149 Among 150 patients with non-epithelioid histology, the median

versus 8.8 months in those receiving chemotherapy (HR, 0.48 [95% CI, 
0.33 to 0.68]).149 The median OS among those treated with nivolumab plus

<1% and PD-L1 ≥1% groups.149 Grade 3 to 4 treatment-related AEs were 
similar in both groups: 31% of patients receiving nivolumab plus 
ipilimumab and 32% of those receiving chemotherapy.148 

Clinical benefit with other chemotherapy agents has also been reported in 
the first-line setting. Cisplatin or carboplatin in combination with 
gemcitabine may be useful for patients who cannot receive pemetrexed; 
partial responses with these regimens have been reported in phase 2 
studies.140-143 Other first-line options include pemetrexed or vinorelbine for 
patients who are not candidates for platinum-based combination 
therapy.144-146 

Pembrolizumab in combination with platinum and pemetrexed 
chemotherapy is also FDA approved as a first-line treatment for adult 
patients with unresectable advanced or metastatic PM.132 The efficacy and 
safety of pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy (pemetrexed 
with cisplatin or carboplatin) versus chemotherapy alone in the first-line 
setting was evaluated in 440 patients with advanced PM in a randomized 
phase 3 trial.150 Epithelioid histology represented over 75% of the study 
population. The median OS was significantly longer with pembrolizumab 
and chemotherapy than with chemotherapy alone (17.3 vs. 16.1 months; 
HR, 0.79; P = .0324). Subgroup data indicate that there was a survival 
benefit with pembrolizumab and chemotherapy regardless of PD-L1 levels. 

More recently, two immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-containing regimens 
have demonstrated efficacy in the treatment of PM in the first-line setting. 
Nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab is approved by the FDA for the 
treatment of adult patients with unresectable PM as a first-line 
treatment.132 This approval was based on data from CheckMate 743, a

Data from both trials evaluating first-line ICI regimens showed that 
immunotherapy led to similar OS outcomes regardless of histology. In 
contrast, non-epithelioid PM appeared to be less chemosensitive than 
epithelioid PM; chemotherapy only regimens resulted in worse survival 
outcomes in the non-epithelioid subgroup than the epithelioid subgroup in 
both trials. Therefore, ICI-based therapy is favored for PM with non-
epithelioid histology. 

The NCCN Panel also recommends (carboplatin or cisplatin)/pemetrexed 
with or without bevacizumab as category 1 first-line therapy options for 
patients with PM. These are included in the NCCN Guidelines as 
Preferred options for PM with epithelioid histology, and as Other 
Recommended options for PM with biphasic or sarcomatoid histology. An 
FDA-approved biosimilar is an appropriate substitute for bevacizumab. 
The Panel recommends the following as regimens that may be Useful in 
Certain Circumstances, regardless of histology: 1) (carboplatin or 
cisplatin)/gemcitabine; 2) pemetrexed; or 3) vinorelbine. 

Not all chemoimmunotherapy regimens confer a clear survival benefit over 
standard chemotherapy. In the randomized phase 3 BEAT-meso trial, 400 
patients with advanced PM were randomized to receive atezolizumab plus 
carboplatin/pemetrexed and bevacizumab or carboplatin/pemetrexed and 
bevacizumab alone as first-line therapy.151 The median OS was 20.5 
months in the atezolizumab plus carboplatin/pemetrexed and 
bevacizumab arm and 18.1 months in the carboplatin/pemetrexed and 
bevacizumab arm; however, this difference in OS was not statistically 
significant (HR, 0.84; P = .14). Given these data, atezolizumab in 
combination with chemotherapy is not included in the Guidelines as a 
treatment option. 

All regimens recommended for PM can also be used for pericardial 
mesothelioma and tunica vaginalis testis mesothelioma; however, these 
recommendations are based on clinical evidence extrapolated from PM 
due to the limited availability of prospective data in these rare 
mesotheliomas.155,156 Broad molecular tumor profiling is recommended by 
the NCCN Panel with the goal of identifying rare driver alterations (eg, 
NTRK or ALK) for which effective drugs may be available or to 
appropriately counsel patients regarding the availability of clinical trials.121 
Refer to the Principles of Systemic Therapy (PM-C 1 of 3) within the 
algorithm for a complete list of recommended systemic therapy options for 
PM.

The approach to subsequent therapy in patients with PM has generally not 
been well established due to limited data from randomized clinical trials;

There is clinical evidence to support the use of other chemotherapy-based 
regimens for the treatment of PM in the subsequent-line setting. One 
phase 3 randomized trial assessed pemetrexed plus best supportive care 
as subsequent therapy versus best supportive care alone in 243 patients 
with PM after progression on chemotherapy (excluding pemetrexed).160 
The difference in median OS was not statistically significant between the 
arms (8.4 months for pemetrexed and supportive care vs. 9.7 months for 
supportive care only; P = .74); however, this result may be explained in 
part due to the design of the study, as patients could cross over to 
pemetrexed. 

The clinical benefit of nivolumab (with or without ipilimumab) as 
subsequent systemic therapy for patients with PM who have not received 
prior immunotherapy was demonstrated in several trials.157-159 The phase 3 
randomized controlled CONFIRM trial assessed nivolumab (67%) versus 
placebo (33%) in 332 patients with mesothelioma after progression on 
platinum-based chemotherapy.157 Most patients had PM (95%) and 
epithelioid histology (88%). Median OS was 10.2 months in the nivolumab 
group versus 6.9 months in those receiving placebo (HR, 0.69; P = .009). 
A clinical benefit was observed regardless of PD-L1 expression status. 
Diarrhea and infusion-related reactions were the most common grade 3 or 
higher AEs reported with nivolumab. Serious AEs were similar between 
the groups (41% for nivolumab vs. 44% for placebo). 

Single-agent vinorelbine and single-agent gemcitabine may also be given 
as subsequent therapy for patients with PM.161-165 PROMISE-meso, a 
multicenter phase 3 randomized trial, assessed pembrolizumab versus 
either gemcitabine or vinorelbine as subsequent therapy in 144 patients 
with PM following disease progression on platinum-based 
chemotherapy.165 There was no significant difference in OS between the 
groups (HR, 1.12; P = .59). Based on the data from this trial and other 
published studies, the Panel continues to support the inclusion of single-
agent vinorelbine and single-agent gemcitabine rather than single-agent 
pembrolizumab as subsequent therapy options. 

A phase 2 randomized trial (IFCT-1501 MAPS2) assessed nivolumab with 
or without ipilimumab as subsequent therapy for 125 patients with PM who 
previously received platinum-based therapy in combination with 
pemetrexed.158 Within the intention-to-treat population, the 12-week 
disease control rate (DCR) was 40% in the nivolumab/ipilimumab group 
and 52% in the nivolumab only group. The median OS reported in this 
non-comparative trial was 15.9 months in the nivolumab/ipilimumab arm 
and 11.9 months with nivolumab alone.158 High PD-L1 expression ≥25% 
was associated with greater overall response based on an exploratory 
analysis of trial data; however, only a few patients had ≥50% PD-L1 levels. 
There were more grade 3 to 4 AEs with nivolumab/ipilimumab than with 
nivolumab alone (26% vs. 14%).158 

The phase 2 randomized RAMES trial evaluated gemcitabine with placebo 
versus gemcitabine with ramucirumab as subsequent therapy in 161 
patients with PM after progression on platinum/pemetrexed 
chemotherapy.162 The median OS was significantly longer in patients who 
received both gemcitabine and ramucirumab than in those who received 
gemcitabine and placebo (13.8 vs. 7.5 months; HR, 0.71; P = .028). Grade

For patients who received pemetrexed as part of first-line therapy, re-
challenge may be effective for certain patients, particularly if there was a 
good disease response following first-line pemetrexed.166,167 A 
retrospective multicenter database study found that rechallenging with a 
pemetrexed/platinum regimen reduced the risk of death when compared 
with rechallenging with pemetrexed alone (HR, 0.11; P < .001).167 

For eligible patients with PM who undergo surgical evaluation and are 
deemed candidates, the goal of cytoreductive surgery is to achieve 
macroscopic complete resection by removing all visible or palpable 
tumors.168 If macroscopic complete resection is not possible, such as in 
the presence of multiple sites of chest wall invasion, then surgery should 
be aborted. However, surgery should be continued if most of the gross 
disease can be removed to help with postoperative management and if 
there will be minimal impact on morbidity. 

NCCN Recommendations 
If chemotherapy (and no immunotherapy) was administered as first-line 
therapy, the NCCN Panel recommends nivolumab with or without 
ipilimumab as Preferred subsequent therapy options, regardless of 
histology. For nivolumab monotherapy, nivolumab and hyaluronidase-nvhy 
subcutaneous injection may be substituted for the IV formulation. 

Rechallenge with pemetrexed-based therapy can also be considered if 
there was a good response to front-line pemetrexed-based therapy. 

Two types of cytoreductive surgical procedures are generally used to treat 
patients with PM: pleurectomy/decortication (P/D) and extrapleural 
pneumonectomy (EPP).168 P/D, also known as total pleurectomy, is a 
lung-sparing approach that involves the complete removal of the involved 
pleura and all gross tumor with or without en-bloc resection of the 
pericardium and/or diaphragm. Extended P/D consists of resection of the 
diaphragm and pericardium in addition to total pleurectomy. EPP refers to 
en-bloc resection of the involved pleura, lung, ipsilateral diaphragm, and 
often the pericardium (see Principles of Surgery in the algorithm). 
Mediastinal nodal dissection should be performed with a goal of obtaining 
at least three nodal stations (see the NCCN Guidelines for Non-Small Cell 
Lung Cancer, available at www.NCCN.org). 

If ipilimumab/nivolumab combination therapy was administered as first-line 
therapy, the Panel recommends (carboplatin or cisplatin)/pemetrexed (with 
or without bevacizumab) as Preferred subsequent therapy options. 

The other subsequent therapy options recommended by the NCCN Panel 
are: 1) pemetrexed (category 1); 2) vinorelbine; or 3) gemcitabine (with or 
without ramucirumab). 

See Principles of Systemic Therapy (PM-C 1 of 3) within the algorithm for 
a complete list of recommended systemic therapy options for PM. 

The choice of surgery for PM was previously controversial due to limited 
data from randomized controlled trials.169-177 EPP is more likely to achieve 
macroscopic complete resection than P/D, but is also associated with 
increased morbidity and mortality.169,172,178-182 Furthermore, the evidence 
supporting the clinical benefit of surgery was mainly derived from case 
studies or non-randomized trials.179,183-185 However, there has been a 
paradigm shift in the treatment of PM based on data from randomized 
clinical trials, which indicated that a non-surgical approach with systemic

Given that routine cytoreductive surgery was linked with increased 
morbidity and mortality rather than a survival benefit in both randomized 
studies, systemic therapy is preferred over surgery as the primary 
treatment modality by the NCCN Panel for most patients with PM. 

The MARS trial was a multicenter study based in the United Kingdom that 
was designed to assess the feasibility of randomizing 50 patients with 
resectable mesothelioma who were candidates for trimodal therapy within 
a 1-year period.187 Patients received 3 cycles of platinum-based 
chemotherapy after initial staging and were randomized to receive either 
EPP or no EPP. The most common chemotherapy regimens used within 
the trial included cisplatin with gemcitabine and cisplatin with pemetrexed. 
Among the 16 patients who underwent EPP, only 8 received postoperative 
hemithoracic RT. There was high morbidity associated with EPP, as the 
12-month survival rate was 52.2% in the EPP group and 73.1% in the no 
EPP group (HR, 1.9; P = .082). The median survival was 14.4 months in 
the EPP group and 19.5 months in the no EPP group. Perioperative 
deaths occurred in 12.5% (3/24) of the EPP group. The median quality-of-
life scores were lower among patients who received EPP compared with 
those who did not. Due to the high morbidity rate in the EPP group and the 
low number of randomized patients overall, the authors concluded that a 
larger randomized trial was not feasible. Noted limitations of the MARS 
trial include low statistical power due to the small sample size, lack of 
standardized chemotherapy regimens, and poor protocol compliance.189 

However, the Panel acknowledges that surgery remains an option for 
select individuals with clinical stage I PM with epithelioid histology and PS 
0 to 2 following a careful surgical evaluation based on factors such as 
tumor histology, distribution, the patient's pulmonary reserve, and 
availability of adjuvant and intraoperative strategies. If the team 
determines that the patient may benefit from resection following surgical 
evaluation, then P/D is the recommended surgical option. EPP should only 
be selected in rare circumstances that require careful consideration of the 
total treatment plan that include both the patient and multidisciplinary 
team.179,187,191,192

P/D) in combination with chemotherapy versus those who received 
chemotherapy alone.188,190 Patients who were deemed surgically 
resectable received 2 cycles of platinum chemotherapy with pemetrexed

Radiation Therapy 

Based on the results from these studies, the NCCN Panel recommends 
that pleural IMRT can be considered as part of primary treatment following 
systemic therapy (induction or adjuvant) with or without P/D in select 
patients with stage I PM with epithelioid histology. Given the technical 
difficulty associated with this treatment, the NCCN Panel emphasizes that 
IMRT should be performed in centers with expertise in this technique. The 
most appropriate timing of delivering RT (ie, after surgical intervention, 
with [or without] chemotherapy) should be discussed with a 
multidisciplinary team. 

RT can also be used as palliative therapy for relief of chest pain, bronchial 
or esophageal obstruction, or other symptomatic sites associated with PM, 
such as metastases in bone or in the brain (refer to the NCCN Guidelines 
for Central Nervous System Cancers, available at www.NCCN.org).69,79,199-

201 

Patients with PM who have undergone P/D are candidates for RT if they 
have good PS, pulmonary function, and kidney function. However, it can 
be challenging to accurately deliver RT to the entire pleural surface 
without damaging radiosensitive sites, such as the lung and heart, 
especially when the lungs are intact.193 Pleural intensity-modulated RT 
(IMRT), a technique more advanced than standard RT, has been 
evaluated in the context of PM to improve survival outcomes. A phase 3 
randomized trial assessed postoperative radical hemithoracic RT (RHR) 
versus palliative RT given after lung-sparing surgery and chemotherapy in 
108 patients with PM.194 The median OS was longer with RHR than with 
palliative RT (25.6 months vs. 12.4 months; P < .001). The 2-year OS rate 
was 58% in the RHR arm versus 28% in the palliative RT arm (HR, 0.54; P 
= .031). In the RHR arm, 11 patients had grade ≥3 acute toxicity; 17 
patients had grade 3 to 4 late toxicity. Nine patients experienced grade ≥2 
pneumonitis. 

CT simulation–guided planning using either IMRT or conventional 
photon/electron RT is acceptable.202-205 For treatment planning, PET scans 
can be used as indicated.201 The clinical target volumes should be 
reviewed with the thoracic surgeon to ensure coverage of all the volumes 
at risk. 

A phase 2 trial (IMPRINT) evaluated the safety of hemithoracic pleural 
IMRT in patients with PM, given after chemotherapy (pemetrexed in 
combination with cisplatin or carboplatin) and P/D.195 Patients in the study 
whose tumors were deemed unresectable after chemotherapy were

received pleural hemithoracic IMRT, grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis was 
reported in 30%; improvement was reported with prednisone initiation. The 
2-year OS was 59% in patients with resectable tumors and 25% in those 
with unresectable disease. Mediastinal nodal failure occurred in 22%

Treatment for patients diagnosed with PM is generally guided by clinical 
disease stage, histological subtype, and operability. Early referral to a 
multidisciplinary team with experience in mesothelioma is recommended. 
The following sections detail treatment recommendations for patients with 
good PS (0–2). Recommendations are stratified by clinical staging; for 
patients who undergo surgery, upstaging may occur. The Guidelines 
adhere to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 9th edition 
TNM staging system.231 

Pleural IMRT is a highly conformal RT approach with improved coverage 
to the hemithorax at risk.197,200,204 Advanced technologies may be used, 
such as image-guided RT (IGRT) for treatments involving IMRT, 
stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), stereotactic body RT (SBRT), and 
intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT).71,193,201,214,215 RT to the 
contralateral uninvolved lung should be minimized,200,216,217 because fatal 
pneumonitis may occur with IMRT if strict limits are not applied.218-220 The 
contralateral uninvolved mean lung dose should be kept as low as 
possible, preferably <8.5 Gy.201,221 The volume of contralateral lung 
receiving low-dose RT (eg, 5 Gy) should be minimized.194,222,223 

For patients with PS 3 or 4, the NCCN Panel recommends best supportive 
care. RT and image-guided thermal ablation are palliative options for 
symptomatic pleural disease.225,232,233 Refer to the Principles of Radiation 
Therapy and the Principles of Supportive Care and Survivorship in the 
algorithm for additional information. 

Pleural effusion can cause discomfort for patients with PM. Thoracoscopic 
pleurodesis or placement of a drainage catheter can be used to manage 
pleural effusion.86-90,94,234-236 Therapeutic/palliative thoracentesis can also 
be used to remove pleural fluid and thus decrease dyspnea either before 
treatment or for patients who are not candidates for more aggressive 
treatment.69 

Clinical Stage I PM with Epithelioid Histology 

It has been controversial whether immediate (prophylactic) RT is useful for 
preventing instrument-tract recurrence after pleural intervention.224-229 The 
phase 3 randomized SMART trial evaluated prophylactic radiotherapy 
versus deferred radiotherapy to assess the rate of recurrences in patients 
who had undergone pleural interventions for PM.230 Patients in the 
deferred RT arm did not receive RT until procedure-tract metastases were 
evident. Among the 203 patients included in the intent-to-treat analysis, 
there was no significant difference in the proportion of those who 
experienced procedure-tract recurrence in the prophylactic RT arm (9%) 
versus the deferred RT arm (16%) (odds ratio [OR], 0.51; P =.14). 
Prophylactic RT also did not improve quality of life, decrease chest pain, 
or decrease the need for analgesic drugs. However, if patients did not 
receive chemotherapy, prophylactic RT did decrease the risk for 
procedure-tract metastases (OR, 0.16; P = .021). The NCCN Panel does 
not routinely recommend prophylactic RT to prevent instrument-tract

epithelioid histology based on available clinical data.202,237-239 Given the

Due to the risks associated with surgery, observation for progression may 
also be considered for patients with PS 0 to 2 who are asymptomatic with 
minimal burden of disease, if systemic therapy is planned when 
symptomatic or radiographic progression occurs. 

The NCCN Panel recommends that systemic therapy can be given as 
either induction or adjuvant therapy if the patient will undergo surgery (see 
PM-3 in the algorithm). Studies assessing multimodal therapy for PM have 
generally included platinum-based chemotherapy regimens.187,188,239 Data 
on the perioperative use of immunotherapy regimens for PM are limited; 
trials to evaluate the use of perioperative immunotherapy and 
chemoimmunotherapy are ongoing.243 

Sequential pleural IMRT at a center with experience in this technique can 
also be considered after surgery and/or systemic therapy as it may 
improve survival outcomes.195,198 Please refer to PM-3 in the algorithm and 
the Radiation Therapy section for additional information. 

Systemic therapy is recommended by the NCCN Panel upon disease 
progression. Refer to the Systemic Therapy section for details on specific 
systemic therapy regimens. 

Clinical Stage II-IV PM with Epithelioid Histology; Sarcomatoid or 
Biphasic Histology (Any Stage); or Medically Inoperable 

Surgical evaluation for potential resection should be considered only for 
certain patients with clinical stage I PM and epithelioid histology who are 
medically operable and can tolerate the risks associated with surgery (see 
PM-2 in the algorithm). The NCCN Panel notes that the benefit of surgical 
resection in PM is unclear and there is no evidence that patient survival is 
improved with surgery when combined with systemic therapy versus 
systemic therapy alone. It is essential that patients receive a careful 
assessment that includes FDG-PET/CT and invasive mediastinal staging 
before surgery is performed (as described in the Pretreatment Evaluation 
section). If surgery is deemed a viable treatment option following surgical 
evaluation by the multidisciplinary team, then the NCCN Panel 
recommends P/D over EPP (see PM-3 in the algorithm). Additional factors 
to consider before treatment selection in this group of patients include the 
extent of disease burden, comorbidities, and patient preference. 

The NCCN Panel currently recommends systemic therapy for patients with 
PM and PS 0 to 2 for those who are medically inoperable or refuse 
surgery, those with clinical stage II to IV PM (regardless of histology), or 
those with sarcomatoid or biphasic histology (regardless of clinical stage)

For patients with sarcomatoid or biphasic histology, surgery is associated

versus no surgery reported in the MARS and MARS2 trials as described 
above,187,188 the NCCN Panel no longer recommends surgery as a 
treatment option for patients with stage II to IIIA PM and epithelioid

strategy for each patient. Factors such as clinical stage of disease, 
medical operability, histological subtype, and PS should be taken into

pleural_mesothelioma_diagnosed.definition: True if the case states that the patient has a diagnosis of pleural mesothelioma.

recurrent_pleural_effusion_or_thickening.definition: True if the case states recurrent pleural effusion and/or pleural thickening.

clinical_t_category.definition: Clinical T category of the primary pleural tumor as stated in the case.

clinical_n_category.definition: Clinical N category as stated in the case.

clinical_m_category.definition: Clinical M category as stated in the case.

histology.definition: Histologic subtype of the mesothelioma as stated in the case.

medically_inoperable.definition: Clinician judgement that the patient is medically inoperable (cannot tolerate surgery). Not stated as a fact in case text; set by the treating clinician.

surgically_resectable.definition: Clinician judgement at surgical exploration that the tumor is resectable. Resectability criteria are not included in the schema input, so this is recorded as a judgement.

clinical_stage_group.criteria_source: unverified: staging criteria not printed in schema input; check against the guideline staging table
clinical_stage_group.definition: Clinical stage group from clinical T, N and M categories. Stage I is T1a or T1b with N0 and M0. Stage II to IV is any T2 to T4, any N1 to N3, or M1. Staging criteria were not included in the schema input and should be checked against the guideline staging table.

ct_staging_branch.definition: Branch after chest/abdomen CT. Stage I with epithelioid histology goes to the first branch. Stage II to IV with epithelioid histology, sarcomatoid or biphasic histology at any stage, or medically inoperable patients go to the second branch.
